questions.q: What does an hour of downtime cost on your most important application?
questions.why: Turns recovery features into money the sponsor recognises.
questions.need: The cost of an hour down on the key application is known
questions.how: Put a number on it with the application owner
questions.listen: A number with an owner is a business case. 'It would be bad' means nobody has counted it yet: count it with them.
questions.probe: Who would notice first, a customer or an internal team, and how long before it reached the board?

questions.q: When did you last restore a whole system, not a file, and how long did it take?
questions.why: Untested recovery is the usual gap behind a confident answer.
questions.need: A whole system can be restored in a known time
questions.how: Restore one complete system and time it
questions.listen: Never, or not end to end, is the gap. A timed test in the last quarter is a strength to build on.
questions.probe: What was slower than planned in that restore, and who was waiting for it?

questions.q: How many clusters run outside the main data centre: plants, branches, edge sites?
questions.why: Remote clusters are the ones the central console does not see.
questions.need: Clusters outside the main data centre are known and managed
questions.how: Bring plant, branch and edge clusters under central management
questions.listen: Sites with no local IT staff are where a platform that looks after itself pays most.
questions.probe: How is a failed disk at the furthest site replaced today, and how long does it take?

questions.q: Do you know which virtual machines have no owner and what they run?
questions.why: Unowned machines are skipped by protection and patching.
questions.need: Every virtual machine has an owner and a purpose
questions.how: Tag machines with owners and retire the orphans
questions.listen: If nobody can say, the estate is bigger than it needs to be: the first saving is what can be switched off.
questions.probe: When did anyone last switch off a machine nobody claimed, and what happened?

questions.q: Which workloads have snapshots, and could an administrator account delete them?
questions.why: Snapshots an attacker can delete are not ransomware protection.
questions.need: Important workloads have snapshots that an admin cannot delete
questions.how: Apply protection policies with immutable copies
questions.listen: Yes, or 'not sure', means one stolen account can erase the safety net.
questions.probe: Who holds those administrator accounts, and does deleting a copy need a second person?

questions.q: Is there a second site, and has failover to it been run end to end?
questions.why: Replication without a tested recovery plan is a hope.
questions.need: Failover to a second site has been run end to end
questions.how: Run a test failover of one application
questions.listen: A runbook that has never been run end to end is a hope, not a plan.
questions.probe: What would you rather the auditor did not see in your last failover test?

questions.q: How far behind on upgrades are you, and what makes upgrading hard?
questions.why: Lifecycle debt is a security risk and the most common hidden effort.
questions.need: Upgrades are routine, not a project
questions.how: Agree an upgrade cadence and remove what makes upgrading hard
questions.listen: Upgrades planned around weekends and change boards cost people every time: that time is the saving.
questions.probe: How many people and nights did the last full upgrade take: firmware, hypervisor and storage?

questions.q: When the platform raises an alert at night, who acts on it?
questions.why: Alerts without an owner turn into noise, then into outages.
questions.need: A platform alert at night reaches someone who acts
questions.how: Route platform alerts to a named on-call owner
questions.listen: A named person with a runbook is mature. 'The supplier calls us', or nobody, means outages last longer than they should.
questions.probe: Which alert last woke someone up, and was it worth it?

questions.q: Which failures must the platform ride through without stopping: a disk, a server, a whole rack, a room?
questions.why: The answer decides how many copies of the data are kept and where they are placed.
questions.need: The failures to survive are agreed, and every copy of the data sits in a different place for each of them
questions.how: Agree the failure domains (server, rack, room) and how many copies each group of workloads needs
questions.listen: This decides how many copies of the data to keep and how much headroom to buy: write it down as a requirement.
questions.probe: Has a whole rack or room ever failed, and what stopped with it?

questions.q: How full are storage and hosts today, and how much room is kept free for a server failure and for growth?
questions.why: A platform run at the edge cannot rebuild after a failure, and the next purchase arrives as an emergency.
questions.need: Capacity is planned with room to rebuild after a failure and to grow, with alerts before it runs short
questions.how: Measure today's use, keep a server's worth of room free, and set alerts at two thresholds
questions.listen: Above about three quarters full, a server failure can leave no room to rebuild: a sizing input, not a detail.
questions.probe: How fast has used capacity grown over the last two years?

questions.q: Which workloads need the fastest storage, and which can live on cheaper capacity?
questions.why: Separating hot from cold data, and deciding where to compress or deduplicate, is where cost and performance are won.
questions.need: Workloads are grouped by the performance they need, with data reduction used where it pays off
questions.how: Group workloads by performance tier and agree where compression and deduplication apply
questions.listen: A few latency-sensitive systems often drive the whole design: name them now so the proof measures them.
questions.probe: Which application owner complains first when storage slows down?

questions.q: Could a tested platform update be pre-approved as routine and run during the working day?
questions.why: Updates that need a weekend get postponed, and a platform that falls behind becomes a risk.
questions.need: Tested platform updates are pre-approved and run during the working day, without downtime
questions.how: Agree with change management a pre-approved path for tested updates
questions.listen: If every update needs a change board at night, simple rolling updates are worth hours a month: agree it as a goal.
questions.probe: What would the change board need to see to treat a tested update as a standard change?

questions.q: What hardware runs the estate today, how old is it, and when does its support end?
questions.why: The end of hardware support is often the real date behind the project.
questions.need: Servers and arrays are listed with their end-of-support dates
questions.how: Export the hardware list with purchase and support dates
questions.listen: An array or a server fleet out of support within 18 months is a reason to decide this year, with a date.
questions.probe: What would it cost to extend support on the oldest array for two more years?

questions.q: Is there a week of performance data for the estate, processor, memory, storage and network, covering the busiest days?
questions.why: Sizing on what machines are given rather than what they use over-buys; a week of peaks sizes it right.
questions.need: A week of performance data covers the busiest days
questions.how: Run a collector for seven days that include month-end or the busiest day
questions.listen: Without measured peaks, sizing falls back on what was allocated, often several times what is used.
questions.probe: Which days of the month are the busiest, and can the collection include one?

questions.q: How much storage belongs to machines that are switched off, and do they still need it?
questions.why: Switched-off machines still hold data: it must be sized, or retired.
questions.need: Switched-off machines are either sized or retired
questions.how: List switched-off machines with their storage and an owner's decision
questions.listen: A large share of switched-off capacity is an early win: retire it before buying for it.
questions.probe: Who can approve retiring a machine that has been off for six months?

questions.q: Which software is licensed per processor core or per host, and does that shape how servers are built?
questions.why: Database and operating system licences can cost more than the platform; they decide the processor choice.
questions.need: Per-core licences are known and the design keeps them on the fewest cores
questions.how: List per-core licences and the hosts they are tied to
questions.listen: Per-core software calls for fewer, faster cores on dedicated hosts. Ignoring it can erase the savings.
questions.probe: What did the last licence true-up or audit cost, and for which product?

questions.q: Which data must be encrypted at rest, and where are encryption keys managed today?
questions.why: Encryption and key management are often a gate in the security review.
questions.need: Encryption at rest and the key manager are agreed with security
questions.how: Ask security for the policy on encryption at rest and key management
questions.listen: A key manager already in place is a requirement to test in the proof, not a footnote.
questions.probe: Who approves a new system that holds encrypted data, and how long does that review take?

questions.q: How many people run the infrastructure, and what would they do with the time if routine work went away?
questions.why: The value of simpler operations is the work it frees, said by the team itself.
questions.need: The team's routine hours are known, and where freed time would go
questions.how: List the routine tasks of a typical month with their hours
questions.listen: A named project waiting for those hours makes the saving real. 'Nothing' means it will not be believed.
questions.probe: Which project was postponed this year for lack of people?
